utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Nice.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your Honour, outstanding from last week is the issue of the intercept. You asked us to deal with it, I think, today. Can I propose the following way of dealing with it, I hope shortly: Arguments about admissibility of intercept in this Tribunal typically -- typically contain two component parts to them: First, the issue of whether there is any illegality according to the domestic law of the country where the intercept was made that could justify its exclusion from evidence; second, whether there's any issue of authenticity that could justify the exclusion of the intercept. In this case, the intercept which is the subject of the evidence identified at paragraph 48 of the summary does give rise to no issues of authenticity because the intercept is between -- is of a conversation between the witness and one other, Karadzic, and the witness is in a position to identify both voices and the conversation itself. That's probably dispositive of any argument, and that may be the view of others in court today. Even if it isn't and we have to go back to the first issue of legality to which sometimes adjoined arguments arising from conventions on human rights generally, it's worth observing the following as a preamble: There can be no question of invasion of privacy here, first because it is the witness himself who is one of the participants in the conversation, and he makes no point on privacy, the other party being a fugitive from justice, Radovan Karadzic, indicted here and failing to attend. That leaves outstanding as the only conceivable argument, a pure legality argument, I understand that which the accused raised last week. Let me make it plain I take no issue with the accused raising the issue late because he had only recent notice of these matters. Nevertheless, there is no substance in any argument of illegality, and the question is how do I make that point? How, if necessary, and at what stage in these proceedings should the matter be explored in detail? It happens by chance that the same Chamber is seized of another case in which the identical point has been raised and in which there has been a very recent filing which is itself public although its annexures are confidential. That's a public filing in the Krajisnik/Plavsic case dated the 27th of September, and so far as material, I read simply from paragraph 10 of that filing of the Prosecution which sets out the following: "On the 23rd of August of 1991, the SDB made a further application to the SRBH Minister for Internal Affairs to intercept the telephone and fax communications of Karadzic." The code name used to refer to Karadzic in the second application was Latas. It goes on to explain that transcripts of intercepts pursued - obtained pursuant to that authorisation are frequently headed with the name Latas, and indeed the transcript we have here is so headed and it is the Prosecution's case that this is the transcript of an intercept obtained lawfully according to the relevant domestic jurisdiction in place at the time. Your Honour, to prove these matters fully and extensively would or will take a considerable period of time and would or will best be an exercise served by pleadings served by all relevant parties in advance, and what I would propose is the following, given the expectation we have that other intercepts will be the subject of evidence before you. My proposal is that this case should be the subject of full pleadings identifying, so far as we can in advance, all the intercepts that we propose to adduce and setting out the legal foundation or the factual foundation for their adduction because we may reasonably assume that the accused will repeat his assertion that Rule 95 is breached. We can do that, I hope, fairly quickly because in large part it will be complete repetition of the position in the Krajisnik/Plavsic case with some additions and perhaps some deletions. If we can do that, with others filing pleadings in response if they judge it appropriate, then we should be in a position to have the matter fully before you in written form, I would hope, ahead of the time, perhaps towards the end of this month, when it's expected that there will next be a witness who will be producing intercepts not only of his own voice, as this witness would do for this single intercept, but also intercepts of others whose voices he can recognise, which may give rise to a slightly more complex consideration. If that course is acceptable to the Chamber, that will simply leave for resolution this particular intercept. I go back to my first point: Authenticity can be proved immediately by this witness. There's no issue of privacy, and that may be dispositive of any objection here today, and we would ask you to admit the intercept. Even if it's not ultimately dispositive of it, the Chamber could admit it on the basis that it will give reconsideration to the topic when all other intercepts are discussed, if they need to be discussed beyond written pleadings, being in a position thereafter to exclude from consideration evidence of these intercepts if it judges that it is indeed in breach of any of the Rules of the Tribunal.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: So the proposal is this: That this matter should be addressed first of all by the Prosecution in writing - and if we were to do that, we would invite the amicus to do the same - that there would be an oral hearing at which the -- all tapes could be addressed, but that meanwhile, this tape should be admitted for the time being - perhaps marked for identification would be an appropriate way to deal with it - the witness can give such evidence as he can about it, but we would decide on its admissibility when we decided on the admissibility of all tapes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your Honour, yes. And of course, has the added advantage -- that course has the added advantage that the same Chamber will find itself dealing at the same time with effectively the same issues in the two cases over which it has oversight, and that, of course, both saves judicial time and ensures consistency of approach.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Nice, all the other intercepts raise the same kind of factual situation, and that's what makes them appropriate to be dealt with together?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: The same kind. I think that we will discover that the majority of intercepts come under the same forms of authority as this one does and as the two categories do identified in the Krajisnik/Plavsic pleading. There are some additional ones which probably have a different factual background and they can conveniently be dealt with at the same time. All intercepts give rise to authenticity issues. Those authenticity issues can be resolved either because it is the witness who will be speaking of his own voice as one of the participating speakers or, alternatively, will be voices he or she can recognise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: One question regarding the specific intercept we have in mind in this case. So the thing is that it is not tape recorded by one of the interlocutors, that is, the witness. So actually, it is an intercept made by a third party, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Correct. It is.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Simply recognised by the witness as his own voice.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We would wish to be addressed in due course, of course, on the jurisprudence, but it occurs to me that this Trial Chamber as it was then constituted in Kordic dealt with not precisely a similar matter but there was a telephone conversation which was intercepted, and the issue about eavesdropping was raised, and I remember we made, I think, an oral ruling on that.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your Honour's recollection is absolutely correct. I can take you to the passages but, to save time, wasn't going to this morning. It starts at 13653. That's not the official version but it's of that order. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: It's about there.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: It's about there, and we can take you directly to the reference.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Kay, is there anything you want to say about that particular course?

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Yes, it's a Rule 95 issue here what that has to obviously be carefully considered because the accused has taken a point against it. At this stage, we don't know the provenance of any of the intercepts. We've been tracking them in the material as they've come in to see that they arise, so to speak, and it's been difficult to link them with particular witnesses within the existing framework of the case. So it would be helpful to start this from the basis of a schedule, the Prosecution setting out their case and then us being able to look at it and decide whether there are indeed Rule 95 issues that there may be on these particular issues.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: And can you see any objection to the course which is proposed about this witness dealing with this particular intercept, marking it for identification, and then the Trial Chamber in due course ruling upon the admissibility when we've heard the rest of the evidence?

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Yes. It's not in evidence until it's ruled by the Trial Chamber as being in evidence. So until that moment, it purely exists as an adjunct to the proceedings.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. But rather than have the witness back to deal with it when we're ready, it may be sensible to have the witness give his evidence about it today.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Yes. But it being subject to admissibility.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, you've heard what's being proposed. At this stage, since we don't have the information available, that we will not rule on the admissibility of this particular tape, this intercept, that we will rule on them all together, all the intercepts as a matter of principle at one hearing. The Prosecution will, first of all, put in a paper which will set out their case, where they say the intercepts came from and their arguments about it. We will give you and the amicus the opportunity to address us upon it. What is proposed for today is that this witness should give his evidence about the tape and then it be marked for identification and so that he doesn't have to be brought back here unnecessarily, and we will rule on the admissibility of this tape at the same time as we rule on the admissibility of the others. Now, rather than addressing us on the principle, is there anything you want to say about that particular course of action? It means that you will have your opportunity to address us on the admissibility of all of the intercepts together.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] [No translation].

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We're not getting any interpretation.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Can you hear the English channel now?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We hear it now. Will you start again, please.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I say that in spite of the fact that I'm not really interested in the substance of these conversations of theirs, my objection is of a principled nature. All these audio recordings were made on the territory of Bosnia-Herzegovina and on the territory of the republics of the former Yugoslavia. That is not contested. I'm not going into the authenticity of the intercept now, although that can be brought into question as well. It was intercepted illegally, without the authority of the state agency in charge. There is no approval of a single state agency for the electronic surveillance of any one of the conversations or, rather, anything that any one of the participants in these conversations said. I point out once again that I'm not interested in the substance. Whatever is obtained illegally is something that is not allowed according to the domestic law or international law. For example, in the law on the interior in Yugoslavia, in Serbia, there is very clear regulation of this. It says if it is indispensable for criminal proceedings or for security or defence reasons, the Supreme Court can, at the request of the Minister, free from the principle of inviolability of such information certain persons. And these are constitutional tenets --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: I'm going to interrupt you. As I said, we will hear the argument upon it in due course. The only point we're deciding at the moment is as to whether there would be any prejudice in ruling on the admissibility of this tape -- hearing the evidence today but ruling on the admissibility at a later occasion. That's really the only point that we're deciding just at the moment. Have you any objection to that course being followed?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, that's precisely what I've been speaking about. What I say pertains to this witness and to other witnesses, because --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Let us consider for a moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We're going to follow the procedure which is proposed, namely, that this intercept at the moment will be simply marked for identification, the witness can give his evidence about it, we will rule on its admissibility in due course when we have ruled on the admissibility of all the intercepts, when we have the Prosecution paper and a response in writing from the amicus, the accused if he wishes to make it, and we've heard oral argument on the topic at a date to be fixed. Yes, Ms. Uertz-Retzlaff.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Good morning, Witness.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-O37 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We had got to paragraph 62, I think it was.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. But I would actually like to raise the intercept issue now with the witness, and it's paragraph 48. And for this reason, I would like -- I would like to request private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: With the help of the usher I would -- we are now moving forward to the section Crimes in the Indictment. It's paragraph 62 in the summary. With the help of the usher, I would like to show the witness the Exhibit -- the map C341, and it is tab 4 in the binder.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Witness, you have here a map with blue lines, and the map -- what do the blue lines show? Can you explain that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-O37 [Resumed]
utterances.text: The blue lines show the area which the Serbs had under their control.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: What is the name of the area that -- where you -- on the left-hand side where you find the names Nadin, Saborsko, Skabrnje, and Bacin?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-O37 [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is the Krajina area. This is the Western Slavonia area, and this is the Slavonia, Baranja, and Western Srem area.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Thank you. With the help of the usher, I would like now to show the witness the map 342, and it's tab 5. Witness, you see now red lines in addition to the blue lines that you just explained before. Can you explain the red lines?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-O37 [Resumed]
utterances.text: The meaning of the red lines is as follows: This was an area which remained under the control of the Serbs at the end of 1991 and right up until 1995.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: With the help of the usher, I would like now to show the witness the map C338, and it's tab 2.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Witness, can you explain this red zone that is encircled here on this map?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-O37 [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's the area which the Serbs at the beginning of 1991 held under their control.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: You said beginning 1991?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-O37 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: When was that taken under control? By what acts?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-O37 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, those were the headquarters and staffs of the Territorial Defence in mid-August, with their soldiers, and they occupied that area and held it under their control.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: With the help of the usher, I would like now to show the witness the map 343, and it is tab 6.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Ms. Uertz-Retzlaff, it may be helpful - it may be that there is such a map, but I don't think we have one at the moment - if we could have an unmarked map of this particular area. I'm looking at tab 2. But the area of the three SAOs in an unmarked form. Don't deal with it now, but at some stage it may be helpful just to have a plain map of the whole area.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. We will produce it.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Looking at the map C343, can you explain this map?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-O37 [Resumed]
utterances.text: This map shows the individual localities, and it describes their ethnic composition. The blue were locations where the Serbs had the majority, and the orange indicates the ratio, how many Serbs and how many non-Serbs or, rather, how many Croats living in the area.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And looking to Western Slavonia, the places that are here highlighted, Bacin, Balinci, Corlug and Cetekovac, would they be correct on the map?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-O37 [Resumed]
utterances.text: This was introduced for those particular places, so just for those places, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And looking at the SAO Eastern Slavonia, Baranja, and Western Srem and at the SAO Krajina, can you comment on these places as well or do you not know the ethnic composition?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-O37 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know the ethnic composition of that, no.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: With the help of the usher, I would like now Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. to show the witness the map C344, and it's tab 7.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: We have now a regional ethnic distribution map, and could you look at Western Slavonia and tell us whether this is correct.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-O37 [Resumed]
utterances.text: That map shows the municipalities according to statistical data, and it is correct, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Could you comment on the SAO Krajina and the SAO Eastern Slavonia, Baranja and Western Srem?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-O37 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I can't. I don't have all the facts and figures.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Thank you. You can put the map away.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: You mentioned that this zone in red on the map for Western Slavonia, that the Serbs were in control. What authorities were in control there in summer 1991?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-O37 [Resumed]
utterances.text: If you mean in Western Slavonia, that was controlled by the Territorial Defence staffs, only them.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: How -- in what time frame were they in control of this entire area?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-O37 [Resumed]
utterances.text: They controlled the entire area until the 15th of October, and then it became less and less. In Lubicko Polje first and then Dadua [phoen] municipality area, and then Boriska Slatina, Orahovica, and finally, Pakrac. That's how it diminished up until the 24th of December 1991, and then you have that narrow portion which stayed on until 1995.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: During this time, were crimes committed against the civilian Croat population?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-O37 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, they were.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: What was done? What kind of crimes occurred?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-O37 [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the Donji Caglic area, with the entry of part of the Banja Luka Corps, a clash broke out and civilians were killed on that occasion with the assistance, as I heard later on, with the local extremists who recognised and pointed out the Banja Luka Corps. In the Cetekovac area, that region there, the local commander with the Territorial Defence units committed crimes as well as in Balinci. In Balinci and in Bacin, the crimes were perpetrated by the members of the radicals, Seselj's radicals, of course with the support and assistance from domestic extremists. And in the Bucje area, there was a prison there where the civilian Croats were brought in and there were some Serb civilians in the prison there too together with them. A part of them were killed and some of them managed to be taken over by the Banja Luka Corps and they were later on exchanged.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: When you speak of the crimes, except for what happened in Bucje, in these other localities, what occurred? Did anything else than killing occur?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-O37 [Resumed]
utterances.text: You mean in Western Slavonia? Well, I can't remember just now.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: In these regions that were under control, were homes of Croat civilians searched?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-O37 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I heard about that later on, that in Vocin, the civilian homes were searched. Usually some people were suspected of having radio stations and that they were informing the enemy. So that was the first reason. And later on, there was looting.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: How did you hear of these things? You said you later heard.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-O37 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did hear about it, especially in the Vocin area in the end of December, because soon after that there was the great exodus of Serbs from there. So I heard later on from people who were there, and heard about it and conveyed it to others, and that's how I came by that piece of information.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Those who conveyed this information, were they Serbs?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-O37 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I heard this from the Serbs, and I later on heard it from the Croatian media as well.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Were homes looted and destroyed?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-O37 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I heard about the looting. As for the destruction, I didn't hear about that. In Donji Caglic I think they were destroyed.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Were churches destroyed, Catholic churches?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-O37 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, they were.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Where?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-O37 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, this happened in Okucani, for instance, and in Donji Caglic when the Orthodox church in Nova Gradiska was destroyed. As reprisal, this was done in Okucani, this act, and in Donji Caglic. That's what I heard. That was the information I received.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Were Croats expelled from the region?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-O37 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. A part of the population was expelled; the others stayed on.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: How did you get this information?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-O37 [Resumed]
utterances.text: From the local inhabitants who disagreed with it.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: When you say "the local inhabitants who disagreed with it," would that be Serbs?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-O37 [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: With the help of the usher, I would like to show the witness the map C338. That's tab 2 again.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Witness, can you point to the village Vocin?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-O37 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Let me just have a look, please. Here it is.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Do you know which -- whether there were any [microphone not activated].

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-O37 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. That's where the Territorial Defence units were and the volunteers.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And when you say "Territorial Defence units," what does that mean?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-O37 [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the area, the Territorial Defence staff of Podravska Slatina was in place.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Who was the commander?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-O37 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think it was Boro Radosavljevic.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Was he a professional soldier?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-O37 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't think so, no.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And you mentioned the -- you mentioned volunteers. Which kind of volunteers?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-O37 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Seselj's radicals were in that area.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Do you know what happened in Vocin?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-O37 [Resumed]
utterances.text: What I heard was that several days towards the end of the exodus several Croatian families were taken off and killed. I also heard that some Serbs managed to hide the Croats to save them from that fate, but they were unsuccessful.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: When was that? About what time? End of the exodus, what is that for you? Which month?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-O37 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, sometime around the 15th of December, that part was subjected to an exodus. And on the 23rd of December, the exodus from the municipality of Pakrac took place.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And who killed these people?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-O37 [Resumed]
utterances.text: According to what the locals said, it was Seselj's radicals and the local extremists who did that.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And when did you hear of this? At that time?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-O37 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I heard about that sometime round the 17th or 18th of December. Then I heard about it even more later on.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And you said locals told you. What -- who told you? Can you be more precise?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-O37 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, locals told me about it, and later on, during the course of 1992, I heard about this from Mr. Mladen Kulic, who, when he heard about this, asked for an investigation to be carried out so it would be known who had done this. He asked the Territorial Defence headquarters of Podravska Slatina to carry out an investigation. Later on, I also heard about what had happened in Vocin from the Croatian media.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Was there actually an investigation conducted, and if so, with which result?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-O37 [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I can remember, no investigation was carried out because the exodus did take place. And later on, I don't think anything was done. Subsequently, perhaps it was the Croatian police that carried out an investigation.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: You also mentioned Balinci and some other places. Can you point them out on the map?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-O37 [Resumed]
utterances.text: It should be somewhere around here. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And the places, can you show us the places Corlug and Cetekovac?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-O37 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Cetekovac? Here, this is where Cetekovac is.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Do you know what happened there?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-O37 [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I can remember, what was done in Cetekovac was done by the local territorials. As for Balinci, this was done by the local extremists and Seselj's volunteers. That's what I heard.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: When was -- was someone killed in these three places and when?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-O37 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I think it was the beginning of October that people were killed in these villages. Civilians, that is to say, both women and men. I don't know the exact date now, believe me.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And when you say "civilians," do you mean Croats?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-O37 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I mean Croats.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: You also mentioned a place where people were detained, Bucje. Can you point this out on the map?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-O37 [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's right over here.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Can you repeat this, please, because it was not visible. It was not visible.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-O37 [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's right over here.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And what kind of a place was it where this happened? Was it a military installation? Was it a civilian place? What was it?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-O37 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Bucje is a Serb village. There are no military installations there. The prison was in private houses. Before, it was allegedly some kind of a school, an old house at any rate. There were no military installations, though.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Who was in charge of this place when people were detained there?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-O37 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know that. That I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Were Croats detained there, civilians, soldiers? Who was detained?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-O37 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Croats were bought there, Croat civilians. I don't know about soldiers. I can't remember. I didn't hear about that. But Serb civilians were brought too, those who the commanders in the area did not like.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: What does that mean they did not like? Had they committed any offences?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-O37 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not hear of any offences, misdemeanors, or crimes. They just protested against the conduct of the local commanders, and then they took them into custody, into those prisons. That's what I heard from people who had been in that prison.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: How long were people detained? In what time period were people detained in Bucje?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-O37 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I don't know. From the beginning -- from the end of August, rather, until roughly the end of November when again, I don't know which way, but they did take them to Stara Gradiska, the Banja Luka Corps did, and then there was an exchange there.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Was there also a detention facility in Gradiska -- in Gradiska?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-O37 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, in Stara Gradiska there is a prison facility. It's there right now and it's been there for the past several decades.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Can you point this place out on the map?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-O37 [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's somewhere around here. Around here. You can't see it.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Is this in Bosnia or Western Slavonia?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-O37 [Resumed]
utterances.text: In Western Slavonia. I see now that the red lines have to be extended to the Sava River. I can't see very well. And the road also has to be extended towards the Sava River, and that's where the boundary is, around this line here. This is where the road is and this is where the boundary is. So these lines should be extended. I didn't notice that until now when I had a more careful look.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Can you point out to us in which part of this territory the Banja Luka Corps was, as you mentioned, from September onwards?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-O37 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Approximately here and then down here, this area.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Were crimes against civilian Croats committed in this region when the Banja Luka Corps was there?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-O37 [Resumed]
utterances.text: In this area here around Stara Gradiska and on the road leading to Okucani, when there was a fighting, then civilians lost their lives as well. But that was in the heat of the fighting, so I don't know under which circumstances this happened exactly.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you. That should be enough with the map. Just one more question in relation to the map. Sorry. This -- we wouldn't need the map. We wouldn't need the map for this. There is this red line -- there was this red line in the -- in the map. This red line, was it based on something you did?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-O37 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Did you --

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-O37 [Resumed]
utterances.text: You mean what I drew? Oh, I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-O37 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I drew that.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: With the help of the usher, I would like to show the witness now the Exhibit C2747, and it's tab 2. Oh, sorry. It's tab 11.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Witness, it is a report of the military post Banja Luka security organ to the military prosecutor in Banja Luka, dated the 23rd of March, 1992. And there is a person signing for this on the last page, Milan Stevilovic. Do you know this person?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-O37 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Milan Stevilovic. I heard of him, and I saw him once at the beginning of 1992, sometime in February, towards the end of February, 1992, in the area of Stara Gradiska.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: What was his position? What did he do?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-O37 [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I can remember, he was head of security for the Banja Luka Corps.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: For which time period was he in this position? Do you know that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-O37 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know about that. I just know that at the time they said that he held that position. I don't know from when until when.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Do you know what happened to him later?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-O37 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I heard that he was killed in an ambush later somewhere in Bosnia, that he was killed by some Serbs who had disagreed with him.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: How -- who told you? How did you get this information?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-O37 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, quite a bit was said about this in public. The military people were talking about it a lot. People were talking about it in general.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And you said that some Serbs had disagreed with him. With what did they disagree? Do you know that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-O37 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, because he carried out various investigations, investigations about killings but also about crime. They say that he did this very staunchly and in a very professional manner.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Looking at this report from him, he has listed here 11 persons. Do you know these persons or have you ever met them or heard anything about them?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-O37 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I don't know these people by name, but according to what I read about later, they belong to the group of Seselj's radicals. I don't know them by name, but I do remember this Stojan Bojanic looted, killed in Glavica. I know that this was done then by Seselj's radicals who were withdrawing, but I don't know them by name.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: You said you heard that. When did you get this information and what information was it?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-O37 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, as for the first information I got concerning this killing, it was already on the 21st or 22nd of December. As for Vocin, I said that I heard about that later. As for Brusnik, what is mentioned here, the Serb village where shells were thrown, I heard about that only later, in January 1992. The situation was chaotic then. As they were withdrawing, you heard different stories about what they had experienced, what they had seen, what they had heard had happened. So I heard about that as they were withdrawing, heard about them too.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: All the places that are listed here in the report - Glavica, Brusnik, Vocin, Kamensko - are they all in Western Slavonia?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-O37 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. All of that is in the area of Western Slavonia. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And the incidents that are listed here, are the victims of these incidents Croats or Serbs or both?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-O37 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Victims are both Croats and Serbs.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Do you know whether anyone was convicted later on for these crimes?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-O37 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't hear about any such thing. You mean this group here? I didn't hear about that, but I heard that some Serbs were later convicted and were in Croat prisons.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Does that mean they were convicted by Croats later, by the Croatian authorities later on?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-O37 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Some Serbs, yes, but not from this list.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Do you know whether any Serbs were convicted for these crimes in -- by Serb courts or Serbian authorities?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-O37 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not hear about any such thing.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: I would like to have the Exhibit C2768 shown to the witness. And it's tab 12. You have here, Witness, a report from the MUP -- the Ministry of Interior of Croatia, and there is a reference in this to the persons Borivoje Lukic and Borivoje Radosavljevic. Did you ever get any information that these persons were involved in crimes in Vocin?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-O37 [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I can remember, this was ascribed to Borivoje Lukic more, although they did speak about this Radosavljevic as well. However, this was ascribed mainly to Borivoje Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Who was Borivoje Lukic? Who is he?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-O37 [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was a local man there. That is to say he lived there in the municipality of Podravska Slatina. He was one of the commanders. I don't know of which unit, but he was one of the commanders. I saw him later. I met him later, as a matter of fact, in 1992.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And you have mentioned here in this report four places where it says training camps. It's Sekulinci, Bucje, Zvecevo and Ceralije. What kind of places were these?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-O37 [Resumed]
utterances.text: These were villages in the territory of Western Slavonia. As for these bases, I did not hear about them but I know that there were TO commands in these places later.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And you have already mentioned Bucje, that people were detained there. What about these other three places? Were people detained in these places as well, Croatians?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-O37 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I heard about Ceralije. I don't know about Sekulinci. I don't know about Zvecevo either.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: In these places, in these four places, were Seselj's men stationed there? Do you know?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-O37 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not at Bucje but in the area from Zvecevo -- I don't know. In Ceralije they weren't there, they were somewhere from Zvecevo towards Slatina, I don't know which area exactly, but they were stationed somewhere in that area.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Yes. That's enough with the document, thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is not clear to me. These documents like the one that was displayed just now, are they being admitted into evidence or does the other side use them only to establish what he had actually stated?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: They're being admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't understand this, then, because the answers -- or, rather, I didn't understand many others before. The answers of this witness are that he had heard something, that he does not know, that he does not remember, and so on and so forth; that he assumes. I don't see how anything can be admitted on that basis, on the basis of his testimony, how anything could be admitted into evidence. It's a different thing if you want to admit into evidence here the entire correspondence of the Croat organs of the interior. That's a different matter altogether. But I don't see how you can tender through this witness things that this witness does not remember, does not recall fully, does not know, had only heard about, et cetera. How can that be admitted at all through him?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: The documents can be admitted because they speak for themselves as documents. As to whether there's any point asking this witness about questions -- about documents about which he knows nothing, that is a reasonable point. Ms. Uertz-Retzlaff, I'm sure you'll have that in mind. If he doesn't know anything about the document, there's really no point asking him anything about it beyond an identification. We are coming to the adjournment, and I must raise with you the question of timing. We've considered the matter, and you can have up until the end of today with this witness in chief, but then we must call that an end, because he will have been giving evidence for something like seven hours by then.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. I will be finished.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: There is another matter, Ms. Uertz-Retzlaff, that you had asked and I believe we might have agreed; to have another witness interposed before the cross-examination. Now, it seems to me that in light of the length of the examination-in-chief, we'll have to reconsider that because I don't imagine it could be reasonable to expect the accused, after seven hours of examination-in-chief, to have another witness interposed and then to have to come back to cross-examination. I think interposing a witness is appropriate where the examination-in-chief is relatively short. Mr. Nice?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: As to that, of course, the other witness is a witness in a quite particular position. He's only available for tomorrow and the day after that. He's coming in today, and I'm afraid arrangements have been made on the basis that his evidence may be interposed, so I very much --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: How long do you anticipate being with that witness in chief?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: A day.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: A day. We've already got a transcript, a substantial transcript.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Yes. It may be less than a day but certainly no longer. I would hope to be less, but we'll see.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: I would invite you to do so. Having read the transcript, there are references to this accused which obviously will have to be dealt with, but for the rest of it, we can rely on the transcript which we've read and thereby shorten at least the examination-in-chief.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Very helpful.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Tapuskovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I would just like to say something. I don't think it is proper to have any break in this witness's testimony because this witness has important things to say in relation to what the next witness will be saying too. I don't think there should be any distinction made between various witnesses here. I believe that the accused will be seriously injured if this witness is not fully heard before the next witness comes in. I really think you should look at that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: In what respect? Can you point to something?

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm convinced that the examination of this witness is relevant to the examination of the next witness too and that the next witness should explain some things probably, I think, in accordance with what I know about this case, after this witness is finished completely. If this is done in the future as well, I believe that it will be to the detriment of validly ascertaining the facts in this case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: You haven't yet given me an example, so it's difficult to judge whether you're right or not, Mr. Tapuskovic, but in any event, the difficulty about the next witness is the position which he holds. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. There is a limit, of course, to what a Tribunal can do to compel witnesses in the position such as the next witness to come, and to some extent we have to accommodate ourselves to their other duties, important duties which they have to perform. Now, we've agreed that he should be interposed. Of course we can always reconsider it. But I don't myself see at the moment, apart from the difficulties which of course there are if a witness is interposed, difficulties for those who have to cross-examine the first witness, but it doesn't seem to me that it's an insuperable task or that it's one which is seriously prejudicial. Having said that, it's not a practice we would encourage. It's only one which should take place in exceptional circumstances. It's not only difficult for those trying to conduct a cross-examination, it's inconvenient for the witnesses. But it must be said that the position of the next witness is one which is wholly exceptional.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I don't want to take up your time, but believe me, it is hard for me to present the arguments why I believe that this witness should be completed first, entirely completed, and that then the next witness be heard. That is very difficult before I do what I think I should do during the cross-examination of this witness, if this is necessary at all, namely if Slobodan Milosevic doesn't deal with that before I do. However, I think that this works to the detriment of the proper establishment of facts. If some witnesses are heard and then interposed and then continued yet again. Of course, it is for you to judge and it is for you to decide on that matter, but it is for me to raise this objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Very well. We will adjourn now. Half an hour -- 20 minutes, rather. The usual adjournment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As the break interrupted what I was saying when I objected, I should just like to comment on one point. You said a moment ago that the documents speak for themselves. Documents can only speak for themselves in the case of an original or when it is an authorised copy, authorised by the Court that it is the same as the original, although not even that bears out the truth of its contents. But I'm just speaking about the form now. Now, this witness is not the author of those documents nor does he know anything about them for those documents to be able to be introduced into evidence on the basis of these copies. And we see through the examination-in-chief that he knows nothing of any substance with respect to the indictment. He's not testifying to the facts, but he is testifying on the basis of some of his political positions and stands. So this long list, I don't know how many tabs and all the rest of it, I can't see the number, cannot be introduced through a witness of this kind.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, that is the common law position which you have enunciated accurately, the old common law position, I might say, which in many jurisdictions has been changed. The old rule was that only a witness who produced a document could in fact produce it in court, that is, one who wrote it or produced it in some way. The law has now moved on from there in most common law jurisdictions. And as far as documents are concerned, as far as official documents are concerned, then they are admissible for what they're worth. Of course they don't necessarily prove that what they say happened happened. That is a matter of weight and a matter to which the Trial Chamber in each case will have to give consideration. But business documents and the like, official documents and the like, are now admissible in many common law jurisdictions, and as far as I know, admissible in all civil law jurisdictions, although I may be wrong about that. However, that is by way of background. In this -- in this jurisdiction, or this Tribunal, we admit hearsay evidence, which of course includes documents. As I said before, they speak for themselves. If there is a real objection to authenticity and there is some ground for that objection apart from just being a general objection, if there is specific ground to say that in a particular case a document is not authentic, then of course that would be considered on being raised by the party making it. So therefore, these documents are admissible for what they contain. As for the contents, that's a matter for the Trial Chamber to consider and decide what weight to give them. Now -- just a moment. Let me finish what I'm going to say. And that concerns the evidence of the witness. If as is happening here, where a witness cannot speak to the document, why, then, he cannot give evidence about it. If there is some point on which you think that evidence should be given, that's a matter which you can raise. And, of course, I remind you that in the course of your evidence -- your case, rather, you can call evidence about documents if you want and call evidence about any aspects of them. So the position is this: That these documents are prima facie admissible, they have been admitted, their weight is for a Trial Chamber to consider, but they're admitted on the basis that official documents and others speak for themselves and it's a matter what weight the Trial Chamber gives to them. We do not have, as I say, a hearsay rule here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, may I say that I found the objection interesting because it sounded so much like a lawyer from the common law jurisdiction, and for that reason I found it quite interesting. But as has been explained, that rule has been overtaken. And in any event, in this jurisdiction we are quite flexible. We admit hearsay evidence. It doesn't mean, of course, that anything and everything goes, but we do have a fairly flexible practice in the admission of evidence which approximates more closely to the system out of which you come, the civil law system.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, we cannot have a debate about this now. That's the ruling of the Court. Now, if you've got any specific objection later on, then of course you can make it about a particular document. I want to deal with a matter with the --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just one brief question, Mr. May, with regard to what you said. You said a moment ago that the witness may introduce as evidence certain documents, and you went on to explain that that is in fact possible. However, unless I'm very much mistaken, all this mass of papers here are not evidence -- is not evidence that the witness is introducing but the opposing party over there, and is introducing through this witness and is asking about them. And that seems to me to be quite specific and cannot be accepted in the way in which you explained. Perhaps I'm mistaken. Perhaps the witness brought in all these documents.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. I've explained and we've given a ruling and the matter is at an end for now. We're not going to engage in a debate on it. But there is one matter. Mr. Nice, we've been considering over the adjournment the position of the interposing of witnesses. We will not disturb the ruling which we gave about the next witness, but on the whole, particularly with long witnesses, it's not a practice which we think should be followed hereafter. We recognise there are difficulties about getting witnesses from abroad in, but where there are long witnesses, it is very difficult for those who have to cross-examine, particularly an accused in person, to cross-examine a witness if there is maybe a lengthy break of two or three days. So could you arrange that in future we don't find ourselves in that position.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: We'll do our best. And indeed, we already are doing our best. It involves a certain amount of negotiation with Victims and Witnesses unit over the length of time that witnesses can stay here, and we have given some thought as to whether there can be reserve witnesses to Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. fill gaps that might otherwise appear in the schedule. Difficult, but we're doing our best.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, regarding the admissibility of the document, if you are going to challenge the authenticity of a document, you need to do it specifically rather than challenging it in general terms as to the content of the document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Uertz-Retzlaff.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. With the help of the usher, I would like to show the Witness the map C2868, and it's tab 8.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Witness, this is a map indicating camps, and it's produced by the Ministry of Health in Croatia. You have already pointed out to us the two camps in Western Slavonia, yet there is a third camp indicated for Western Slavonia. It's called -- it's called Molokivicevo [phoen]. Are you aware that there was a prison camp in this place?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-O37 [Resumed]
utterances.text: You mean Miokovicevo.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-O37 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have heard about Miokovicevo and the fact that some killings occurred there but I didn't know about the camp.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: There are camps indicated in Western Slavonia -- Eastern Slavonia. Do you know any of these camps indicated here? Did you get information about this?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-O37 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I heard about Ovcara and Sarengrad, but I heard about them from the media.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Did you hear -- did you hear it at that time while they existed or a long time afterwards?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-O37 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I heard about them during 1991, approximately in October of that year. And later on as well. I heard more about them later on.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Looking at Krajina, the SAO Krajina, did you get information about camps there?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-O37 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I heard about Knin and Udbina. I heard about the others later.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And these camps in Knin and Udbina, did you get this information at the time when they existed, these camps?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-O37 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Some of them I heard about from the Croatian media during the war. And then later on, as I say, I heard about all the rest, after 1995.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Looking at Bosnia, do you know the camps in Bosnia? Did you get information about any camps in Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: I think we're now going out of the area in which the witness can usefully give evidence unless he was actually in Bosnia and saw some of these camps.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Your Honour, the point that I wish -- would wish to make is the widespread knowledge of these sort of facilities and of crimes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Could I continue?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Did --

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-O37 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I heard about Manjaca at the time from the media, and Banja Luka too.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Did you hear that atrocities were committed or people were killed in these places at that time?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-O37 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I heard that.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Your Honours, I would like now to move on to the point -- paragraph 69 and the following about Seselj.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: You have already mentioned Seselj's men's involvement in the crimes in Vocin. Do you know when Seselj's men arrived in the region of Western Slavonia?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-O37 [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I remember, this was sometime towards the end of September.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Did you actually see them arrive?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-O37 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I saw one group when it arrived in a bus. I didn't know at the time that it was Seselj's men, but that's what I heard later on.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: What did these soldiers look like?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-O37 [Resumed]
utterances.text: They were dressed differently. They had camouflage uniforms on with different insignia and emblems on their caps, on their shoulders, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: What kind of insignia?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-O37 [Resumed]
utterances.text: They had the eagles, flags, and other types of folklore, but mostly it was the eagles.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: You call it folklore. Is there a special term for this kind of folklore signs?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-O37 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, they were signs that the radicals used to sport and wear.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Could you see how these people were armed?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-O37 [Resumed]
utterances.text: They had different types of rifles, short barreled pistols, the Heckler type of short weapon, automatic and semi-automatic rifles as well.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Do you know how they got these weapons?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-O37 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know that.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: When you saw them arrive, did they have these weapons already or were they distributed within the region of Western Slavonia?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-O37 [Resumed]
utterances.text: The group that I saw in the bus didn't have any weapons. Now, I can't say what the other groups had or where they got their weapons from later on.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Did you later on then see these kind of soldiers with weapons? Because you described the weapons.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-O37 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Later on, around the region of Glavica, I saw a group with them.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Those arriving soldiers, were they integrated in -- within the ranks of the TO in the regions or did they always operate separate?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-O37 [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I was able to learn, they were under the TO command of Boriska Slatina. That's who they were with most often. But whether they were a separate unit, I really can't say because I was never in the region, so I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Do you know how they were fed and housed and equipped with other than weapons?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-O37 [Resumed]
utterances.text: They were in the Boriska Slatina region from Zvecevo, to the north of that. How they got their food, I don't know. Whether they had their own kitchens or how they came by their supplies, I really can't say.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Do you know whether these soldiers were paid?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-O37 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: With the help of the usher, I would like now to show the witness Exhibit 2780, and it is a rather lengthy, complex document, but I will only discuss a few pages.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be tab 13.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: The witness has to have the whole stack.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Witness, after your arrival in The Hague, did you have opportunity to look through this rather complex, huge document with all the lists attached to it?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-O37 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: What kind of document, in particular the lists involved with these documents, are these?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-O37 [Resumed]
utterances.text: They are lists of fighters of the Territorial Defence at Zvecevo, Boriska Slatina, et cetera, and I have received a document here - perhaps it was a mistake, it is in English - pertaining to the crimes and the investigation Locin.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: The witness should --

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-O37 [Resumed]
utterances.text: These are lists of TO defence fighters, and the cards, the military records that came from the secretariat, the municipal ones, and they were photocopied and copied out, of the people, the number of weapons, and personal data relating to them.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Do you know who compiled these sort of documents? Are you aware of that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-O37 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Usually they were compiled by people working in the TO defence staffs, and they were also, by virtue of office, employees keeping records Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. in the municipalities.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Having reviewed these documents in detail before the testimony, would you say they are genuine documents?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-O37 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I would.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: I would like now to speak about a few items on this list, and I think it's most helpful if you look into the index, the index list on top of the document. The first item is a special platoon members list. Do you know whether there was a special platoon and what it was doing?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-O37 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I heard that there were several special platoons up there, but what their purpose was I really can't say, but all I know is that it was composed of former policemen, and people liked to brag about being in one of the special platoons.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: There is also, as item 3, the Papuk detachment. What was the Papuk detachment?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-O37 [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Papuk detachment got his name from Papuk Mountain in the Boriska Slatina area, up by Daruvar.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: In the list, there are references to weapons that the certain unit members had. Do you know who provided the weapons to these people?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Do we have a translation of this? I don't seem to have one.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Yes, you should have one.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] What I -- the information I received was that the commanders and the command of the Territorial Defence were provided with weapons. Now, how they came by those weapons, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Your Honour, for your assistance, the entire English translation comes first and then there comes the B/C/S, and it's all numbered with the numbers in the index.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: For some reason mine seems to be missing. Judge Kwon has one, so I can use his. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Witness, please have a look now at item 58, the document 58 of this list. Do you have it?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-O37 [Resumed]
utterances.text: It says 58 here, a list of volunteers from Serbia and the permits.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Yes. The list -- this list dated 9 December 1991, is signed by Rajko Bojcic. Do you know what position Rajko Bojcic had at that time?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-O37 [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was one of the local commanders. I don't know which unit and headquarters he belonged to.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And you have -- the document includes a list of 38 persons of the Serbian Radical Party going on leave.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-O37 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I can see that.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And the following pages, 59 is another list of members of the Radical Party. Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-O37 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not yet. Just a moment.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: It's identified as 59, and it says, "Volunteers from Serbia, special unit." To make it easier, can I just give you my copy?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-O37 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Here it is. Here it is. We've found it.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And as you can see, there is a list of volunteers from Serbia special unit. Were --

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-O37 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I can see that.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: What kind of unit was this?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-O37 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know about that. As I said, they often called themselves a special unit. They would probably have a special status, therefore. However, what their particular assignments were, I really don't know.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Besides the Seseljs that you have already mentioned, these members of the Serbian Radical Party, were there any other special units from Serbia in the region?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-O37 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, all these units that were from Serbia were said to be Seselj's.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And related to this list of volunteers on the document 19 December, would you have a look at a document dated 10 December 1991, a list of escorts for the fighters going on leave. It does not have a proper index number on it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: How is the witness to find, Ms. Uertz-Retzlaff?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I can see that.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And it refers to a list of escorts for the fighters going on leave, destination Vocin, Banja Luka, and back. Was Vocin located in Podravska Slatina municipality?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-O37 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: What was the relation between Vocin and Banja Luka? Can you explain the destination of these fighters going on leave?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-O37 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I don't know where they could have come from. Rajko Dobric should be from Western Slavonia, judging by his surname. Gajic Milan too. They were probably going on leave or to visit their families. I really don't know. But Vocin is Western Slavonia, and Banja Luka, as we know, is in Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Can the witness now have a look at --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mrs. Uertz-Retzlaff, before that, could you establish as to the reason why there is a Croatian stamp there.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: You heard the Judge's question. On these documents, actually on each page there is a Croatian stamp. Do you know why it is there?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-O37 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I think that the Croatian police came in the possession of these documents and, therefore, they marked them as being in their possession.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Do you know anything -- how these documents got in the possession of the Croatian police?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-O37 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the only thing that is possible is that, when there was the exodus, when the people from that area left, as well as the fighters, then these documents stayed behind and they found them.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Your Honour, is that sufficient?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: I would like you to have now a look at a document which is marked 58, and it's an authorisation --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I assume that it's a technical mistake. I'm not really accusing anyone. But in tab 13, I just have one sheet of paper where there are a few names, scouts of the 1st Company, and it has this Croatian stamp. I don't have these lists at all that were quoted a while ago. This is probably a technical error. So could you please give me copies of these documents that have been referred to just now, that are being looked into, so that I could have a look as well.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, these documents were disclosed to you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Well, don't -- don't address him. The documents, no doubt, were disclosed, but if you would assist us by producing another bundle. First of all, in the -- no need to do it now, but make sure he gets it by the end of the day.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, we will do that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Produce a list, if you would, in the B/C/S for him, and I would like an English translation, which I don't seem to have got.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Yes. Sorry, Your Honour, for this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Have we finished with the lists?

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: No. There are several more documents, and it's actually not so much the listing but the documents, letters and authorisations attached to these lists.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: The first I would like to address, the document which is marked 57, and it is a document dated 14 November 1991. Here is a -- we have here -- we can assist you, Usher.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-O37 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Who is signing this document? Have a look at the signature.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-O37 [Resumed]
utterances.text: It says Munja, but I can't know exactly, judging by this signature, who the actual signatory was. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Was there a person with the code name or nickname Munja?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-O37 [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was a person. I think it was either Boro Radosavljevic or this other one. Just a minute. Let me find this so that I can remember. This was used by two or three men. Somebody said it was Veljko Vukovic. Somebody said it was Boro Radosavljevic. So I don't know who it was exactly.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Then I would like you to have a look at the item 58, and it's an authorisation of the 5th of November, 1991, and --

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-O37 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Here it is.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Yes. And it is also signed "Munja" again. And there is a handwritten note on it. Can you read this note to us?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-O37 [Resumed]
utterances.text: "Veljko Vukelic is hiding behind the name of Munja."

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: There is a --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Tapuskovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, on this document, it says "Munja," yes, but there is a handwritten note here stating who it is. So this is a very leading question because the answer is readily available. Please have a look at the document itself. You will see it written down here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. We have the document. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: I would like to continue now with a document which is marked as number 62, and it's an order, an order dated the 27th of September, 1991, from the TO municipal staff Podravska Slatina.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-O37 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I can see that.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Can you tell us who signs this document? Can you identify the signature?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-O37 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I am not receiving any interpretation.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Can you --

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-O37 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I didn't hear any interpretation.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Yes. Can you have a look at the signature. Do you know who signs the document?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-O37 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Now I can hear it.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Yes. Can you identify the signature?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-O37 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Radosavljevic. On other documents, it also said "Radosavljevic" and there was his signature, and now I see this signature again.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And can you read what is written on the stamp?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-O37 [Resumed]
utterances.text: "Podravska Slatina SAO Krajina, the municipal staff of the Territorial Defence."

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: What is written on the outer -- what is the outer wording?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-O37 [Resumed]
utterances.text: It says "The Socialist Federal Republic of Yugoslavia."

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Can you comment on this for us? Why does the stamp have "Socialist Federal Republic of Yugoslavia" and why is there also "SAO Krajina" on it?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-O37 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I don't know. These staffs made their own stamps, their own seals. So they were different. They were not uniform ones. They did not have anything to do with the SAO Krajina, so they put it there by themselves. I don't know. I don't find this clear either, because if you look at the seals and stamps of other units, you will see that they are quite different.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
