utterances.text: And as to the contents of this document, it says here: "Pursuant to the requirements and plans of the SAO Slavonia Main Staff, I order the forming of regional departments of Vocin police station as follows," and there come the departments. Was the SAO TO, was it responsible for the police stations as well or what does that mean that they order something in relation to the police, that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-O37 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, that means -- yes, that means that the Territorial Defence established police stations at the locations where they were in command. They had authority over them.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Since when did the TO have authority over the police stations? Do you know that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-O37 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, they did that from the beginning, from the beginning of the war, depending on the place involved. There were no other authorities, only the Territorial Defence staffs, and then they took over that function as well.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And the next item I would like you to look at is a call-up note. It's also not specifically numbered. It's a call-up note dated the 28th of November, 1991.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-O37 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I an see that.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Were at that time in November 1991, was there a general mobilisation?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-O37 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Oh, no. Again it was the Territorial Defence staffs on their own who put people there who were not on those units. And they carried out this mobilisation on their own in order to place them under their command.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Your Honour, I need half a minute, because I'm actually looking now for a certain document that I can't find myself.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. I can continue. I lost the tab on it.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: It's item 60. Can you please look at item 60, a permit for free movement on the territory of the SAO Krajina Western Slavonia.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-O37 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I can see that document.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Witness, can you say who is giving this authorisation?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-O37 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Again it was issued by Radosavljevic, commander in Podravska Slatina. At that time, such permits for movement in the territory concerned were being issued.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Did people need authorisation to move around?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-O37 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Commanders did not allow soldiers to move about without permits.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Thank you. That was all.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: We can now leave this exhibit, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Witness, before we started to talk about this exhibit, we were speaking about Seselj's men. Did Seselj's men have a certain reputation?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-O37 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, people were rather afraid of them. They were quite rough. They did things to the local population. They were often under the influence. They made threats. Some of them were engaged in looting, at least that's what people told me. People complained to me that they had been robbed. At any rate, the local population distrusted them and feared them.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Did that apply to the Croatians, the Croatian population, the Serbs, or who?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-O37 [Resumed]
utterances.text: This applied both to Serbs and Croats.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Did Vojislav Seselj ever come to the region and visit Seselj's men?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-O37 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. He was there sometime in November 1991, in the area of Zvecevo, and then he went to review his units.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: When you say "review his units," what does that mean?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-O37 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, at that time people said that he came to review his units to see what position they were in, how well equipped they were, to talk to them. He was supposed to review them like any commander who would be lining up his troops.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Do you know where exactly he went in Western Slavonia, where he did that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-O37 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, somewhere between Zvecevo, Vocin, and that area around Podravska Slatina. I don't know the other places involved.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Did he give speeches to the soldiers? Do you know that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-O37 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I heard that he made a speech, that he spoke to them, greeted them.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: You said you heard that. Did you hear him give the speech or did you only hear about the speech?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-O37 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was not there where he was making the speech. That's to say that I could not have heard the speech itself. I heard that he had made a speech.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And who told you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-O37 [Resumed]
utterances.text: People talked about it, the local population, people who were there. And then later on, they talked about it. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Your Honour, I would like now to go into a private session because I want to discuss a matter between this witness and Seselj.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Did the various units -- you have already mentioned that the various units left Western Slavonia at some point in time. When was that? Western Slavonia.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-O37 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the beginning was on the 15th of October, 1991, when the people from Grubisic Polje left. And then towards the end of November, the second half, the people from Daruvar, then Slatina, Orahovac and Pakrac. Most of Pakrac was abandoned on the 23rd, 24th, by the 27th of December. They actually left in several waves, and they were accompanied by the volunteers who were in Slatina. They were also leaving from Slatina. On the 15th of October, they went to Bucje -- no, not the 15th of October, the 15th of November, from Vocin. Vocin. Slatina. Sorry; the 15th of December. It was the 15th of December.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: When the soldiers left, what did the local Serb population do?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-O37 [Resumed]
utterances.text: They left together with them.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Why did they leave? Was there a major offensive of the Croats ongoing or why did they do that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-O37 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Later on, it turned out that there was not a major Croat offensive but the territorials, as they were leaving, I mean the territorials were from the families that lived there. So then when they left, of course they left with their wives and children. Of course they left together. Only a few days later, the Croat units entered these villages. And then they carried out certain actions in these villages, but it was only a few days later.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: When you speak about "certain actions," what do you mean?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-O37 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, then, when the Croat army entered these Serb villages, they also looted the area, torched houses, mined them. Some of the local population was killed and others were taken to prisons.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Your Honour, I would like now to move on to a meeting regarding the Vance Plan, and it needs to be in private session because it's a very particular meeting.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: You mentioned the RSK. When was it established?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-O37 [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the 26th of February in Borovo Selo, near Vukovar.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Was it established -- was there an RSK established in Knin before that date?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-O37 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. It was only the SAO Krajina that was in Knin.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Who was the president of the RSK?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-O37 [Resumed]
utterances.text: The first president was Goran Hadzic.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Before this meeting in Borovo Selo and the establishment of the RSK, was there a meeting in Glina?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-O37 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I heard that a meeting was held in Glina to discuss the Vance Plan. There was the SAO Krajina Assembly there, and the Vance-Owen Plan was accepted.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: On this 26th of February, 1992, the RSK, what was it comprised of in relation to territories?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-O37 [Resumed]
utterances.text: It comprised of the SAO Krajina, Baranja, Western Srem, and the SAO Western Slavonia.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Why did they -- why did Western Slavonia join?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-O37 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Because it saw its chance and seized it, through the Vance Plan, to set up a body for negotiation and that contact be established with the international community. But what we endeavoured to do was to remain our own autonomy, so that we insisted in the -- to join the RSK as a regional entity and as the Serb region of Western Slavonia. And this was introduced into the new RSK laws which provided for its autonomy. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Given your -- given your criticism against Goran Hadzic as a leader, why was he chosen to be president? Do you know that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-O37 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, at that point in time, a substitute for Milan Babic had to be found, and he -- as he was a rather popular person who had emerged from the war and accepted the Vance Plan, then he was to be the president of the republic. And Zdravko Zecevic who was from Benkovac was to be the Prime Minister.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: That appointment of Mr. Hadzic, was it agreed upon in advance of the meeting on the 26th of February?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-O37 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think so, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Who agreed upon this? Do you know that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-O37 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I can't say now. I don't know. I heard that that was the agreement reached, but who actually reached it and between whom, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And how did -- who informed you about this agreement?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-O37 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I heard it at the Assembly on the 26th of February. I think it was from Zdravko Zecevic that I heard it.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Who was the Minister of the Interior of the RSK?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-O37 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Milan Martic.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Was there a Defence Minister, and if so, who was he?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-O37 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, there was. It was Spanovic. Spanovic was the surname. I can't remember his first name just now. Colonel Spanovic, anyway.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Colonel. Was he a professional soldier?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-O37 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, he was. He was an officer of the Yugoslav People's Army. Beforehand, he was from Pakrac by birth, and he spent the war in the Knin area.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Did you have a Minister of Finance?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-O37 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That was Vojislav Peuraca.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Did the government of the RSK have a regular budget?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-O37 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it had to have a budget in order to be able to function and to finance its institutions, services, and departments.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: In which periods? Which budget periods did you have there?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-O37 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, at that time, at the beginning, I think they were quarterly ones and later on were annual budgets.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Do you recall the percentage spent on police and TO in the budget?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-O37 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: What source of income did the RSK have within their own territory?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-O37 [Resumed]
utterances.text: The only source that they could have had was from the timber industry and the little production that they had and from the oil resources in Eastern Slavonia.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: To how much did this amount?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-O37 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. I can't say.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Could the RSK exist on this income gained on their own territory?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-O37 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, it couldn't. It wasn't sufficient.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Where did the funds come from that were needed?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-O37 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the Prime Minister and Finance Minister would go off to Belgrade for talks. I don't know who with, but they did discuss financing aspects.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And as a result of these discussions, did any money arrive? Do you know that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-O37 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I knew that the money was coming in because we received our salaries. All bills were paid. So I don't know how or the amounts of monies that were coming in, but anyway.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: How do you know that the Prime Minister and the Finance Minister would go off to talks in Belgrade? Did they report about this or did they speak about it in advance?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-O37 [Resumed]
utterances.text: At one of the government meetings, they said that they had to go there for negotiations, to discuss the currency, what it was going to be called, what shape it would take, what value it would be set at, that they had to discuss this with the governor of the bank, and they had to go to Belgrade for talks, although these meetings were held in a rather narrow circle, so I never learned the details.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: When was that said? You said they mentioned it in government meetings.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-O37 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, that was already sometime at the beginning of 1992. April, I would say. May perhaps.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Did they go and meet authorities of Serbia or Yugoslavia? Do you know?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-O37 [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I heard, it was the Serbian authorities.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Did Mr. Martic, the Minister of Interior, also go to Belgrade for discussions?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-O37 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, he did. He went too.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: When -- when did he do that and whom did he meet?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-O37 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, right at the beginning when the government was set up and had been formed, he went to Belgrade, but who he met there, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Did he report on his meetings? Did he say what he achieved?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-O37 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I don't remember that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: If that's a convenient moment, we'll take the adjournment. We will adjourn now for 20 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. With the help of the usher, I would like to put to the witness Exhibit C2449, and it's tab 9.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Witness, please have a look at the signature and the stamp of this document. Do you know them?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-O37 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: What is it?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-O37 [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is Spanovic's signature, and the stamp is the government stamp.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: This document refers to a meeting on the 12th of November, 1992, hosted by the president of Serbia. Do you know about this meeting?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-O37 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: At that time, was -- what was the financial situation in the RSK in late autumn 1992?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-O37 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I think there were problems with the salaries of soldiers, that their salaries were very small. I think there was a general lack of money.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And was this general -- was this situation solved afterwards?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-O37 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, there was an ongoing crisis, but it wasn't as bad as it was at that point.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Do you know whether money arrived?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-O37 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: In this document, there is a reference in the second paragraph. It says the president, Mr. Milosevic, agreed to the concept of creating a defence system of the Krajina which would be based upon about 23.000 people in the police of whom 5.000 would be in the regular police and 18.000 in brigades. Do you know about this concept?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-O37 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I heard about these figures, the number of men and police and the regular composition, the brigades, that all this was mentioned, but I don't know the exact quantities, numbers, and their deployment.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: In this document, it's -- a little bit further down in the next paragraph, it says: "President Milosevic said that funds for maintaining equipment should be planned by the army of Yugoslavia, that it would help in the implementation of this, and that the army of Yugoslavia should finance the active officers and civilians who stayed behind in Krajina." Do you know anything about how equipment maintenance was funded, and soldiers?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-O37 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I heard that this went through the army of Yugoslavia. I don't know how, though. This was the first time I see this document. But I did hear that this went through the army of Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And how did you hear it? Where was it?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-O37 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I heard that at one of the government meetings, that the army would be financed through the army of Yugoslavia. This was round the Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. end of 1992 or the beginning of 1993.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: We can put this document away.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And the witness should be given the document C584. That's tab 5.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: This exhibit is a set of three letters, and I would like you to look at the first letter, which is a letter from the president of the republic, Goran Hadzic, to the president of Serbia. Would you please have a look at the signature and the stamp of this document, and can you tell us whether they are genuine?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-O37 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Do you recognise the signature and the stamp?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-O37 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: This letter refers to the staffing needs and assistance in maintenance. Do you -- are you aware of this letter? Were you aware of this letter at that time?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-O37 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. At that time, I was no longer in the Krajina government.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Your Honour, the letter has no date, but there is a date received, 4 June 1993.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Looking at the next letter, it is a letter from the 13th of April, 1993. If you please look for the stamp and the signature. Can you say --

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-O37 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know the signature because I did not know the signature of what it says here, Mile Novakovic, General. As for the stamp, that kind of stamp did exist in the army.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Mile Novakovic, what was his position at that time?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-O37 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, he was commander at that time, commander of the army of Republic of Srpska Krajina.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: The letter is actually to the Minister of the Defence of SRJ. What does that stand for?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-O37 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, that means it was sent to him, to the Minister of Defence of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia, that this letter was sent to him and that he was requested to do what it says here.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: The request relates to officers with a law degree. Are you -- do you know whether there was a need for such officers and whether they actually came?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-O37 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I heard people say that there were quite a few problems, that there were things that needed to be processed legally. I don't know whether that was the case then, because I was no longer active by then so this information was not really accessible to me, especially as far as the army is concerned. I knew hardly anything.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: The next -- the next letter, the last of this exhibit, is a request for this -- is a request for equipment from the 22nd of March, 1993. Would you please have a look at the stamp and the signature.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-O37 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I see that. Again the stamp is not clear to me, and I don't know the signature of Mile Novakovic, as I said, but this is the kind of stamp that the military did use.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you. Before we go to the next document, I have forgotten to ask you something. What currency did you have in the RSK?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-O37 [Resumed]
utterances.text: We had the Krajina dinar, the dinar of the RSK.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: The national bank -- was there a national bank in the RSK?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-O37 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Believe me, I can't remember. I don't know about that.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Can the witness now be given the document C3383, and it's tab 14.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Witness, this is a letter dated the 28th of April, 1993, from Mr. -- Minister Milan Martic to several officers listed on top. Can you please look at the stamp and the signature.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-O37 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have seen both the stamp and the signature. As far as I know, it does correspond to the original. That is what the stamp was, and that is what Martic's signature was like.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Do you recall that there was, at that time, a discussion on the increase of the salaries of the police?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-O37 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. At that time, I was suspended, so I'm not aware of any such talks.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Can the witness now be shown the Exhibit 4236, which is tab 23.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Would you please have a look at the stamps and the signatures on the last page of this document.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-O37 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Again, the signature of Mile Novakovic is not familiar to me because I didn't know his signature. I recognise the stamp of the army, and I also recognise the stamp of the ministry, and also Martic's signature.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Can the witness now be shown Exhibit 4236. Sorry, that was just the one we had. Sorry. 3769.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Tab 17.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Witness, this is a letter of the Ministry of the Interior of the RSK to the Ministry of Interior of Serbia, and would you please have a look at the stamp and the signature.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-O37 [Resumed]
utterances.text: The stamp does correspond to the ministry, but I don't know whose signature it is. I see it is not Martic's signature, it is somebody else's signature.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Thank you. That's enough.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Witness, when did the UN troops arrive in the RSK?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-O37 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I think it was sometime around the beginning of March 1992. That's when they started coming.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: When the UN troops arrived, did the authorities in Western Slavonia cooperate with them?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-O37 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, they did.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: What was done in Western Slavonia in relation to demilitarisation?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-O37 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Western Slavonia carried out demilitarisation, which means that weapons were only carried by policemen round their waists. All the rest were civilians. Marrack Goulding, Under-Secretary of the UN, came in September and gave us recognition for this because we had carried this out on time, and then we could proceed further.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Did you increase the police force in Western Slavonia?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-O37 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. There was no increase. The number of policemen remained the same except for the fact that they were the only ones who carried weapons, namely pistols, on belts around their waists.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Who was the local TO commander?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-O37 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Colonel Jovan Cubric, who took part in the demilitarisation. After that, he was in civilian clothing as well.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Was he replaced at some point in time?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-O37 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. He was replaced in 1993, sometime in the month of April, and he was replaced by Colonel Celeketic, and he established once again an army in the territory of Western Slavonia.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Does that mean after the replacement -- what does it mean? After the replacement of Jovan Cubric, did the demilitarisation come to an end?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-O37 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: This new commander, Celeketic, where did he come from?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-O37 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Celeketic? He came from Yugoslavia. Originally he is from Kikinda.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And what did he do?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-O37 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, then he established staffs once again. Officers wore a uniform again. They were given weapons. People again went on guard duty on positions. He established brigades, units.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: In relation to the Vance Plan in Western Slavonia, did you try to carry out the return of refugees?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-O37 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that was our plan, for the refugees to return. And we negotiated with the representatives of international organisations to do that as well.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Did the Serbs in Western Slavonia accept the reintegration of Western Slavonia into Croatia?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-O37 [Resumed]
utterances.text: They did. They were in favour of that option.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Looking at the former SAO Krajina, did they also work towards demilitarisation?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-O37 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. They did not work towards demilitarisation. Martic wanted to create an army, a strong army and police and hold the borders of the territory under control.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: How do you know that? Did you go there?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-O37 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I was in Knin when he negotiated and quarreled with UN commanders. He did not accept short weapons only. He kept asking for long rifles for the police, as well as heavy machine-guns, and also for the military. He did not accept the solution that we had worked out for Western Slavonia.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Was the police force increased in the former SAO Krajina?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-O37 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I can't say the police when it was the army before the Vance Plan. I can't exactly say what the personnel levels were, but I know that there was quite a bit of army people and the police.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Did Croatia -- did Croatian refugees return to the SAO Krajina? Do you know that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-O37 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, they did not.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: What was the problem?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-O37 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the climate was not right yet, and most of the members of the government thought that there can be no refugee return yet, that all of these things were still fresh, and that it was -- that the situation was not right for the return of the Serbs or of the Croats.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: With the help of the usher, I would like to put to the witness the Exhibit 3765, and it's tab 16.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Witness, this is a letter of the Ministry of Internal Affairs in Knin, dated the 28th of September, 1992. Can you please have a look at the stamp and the signature.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-O37 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I see that somebody signed this instead of Milan Martic. The stamp is the one that corresponds to the ministry.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: There is a reference made in this document to the -- to the immigration of the population for Skabrnje, Novi Grad, and Pridraga. Do you know about this?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-O37 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I heard about that, that the Croats wanted to return to their villages and towns again, the ones where they had lived before. I remember about Skabrnje and Novi Grad. I don't remember about the rest. I also remember about Baranja. Croatia kept exerting pressure for the refugees to their villages and towns.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: In this letter, there is a -- there is mention that the government will be forced to prevent the arrival. Did the government of the RSK prevent the arrival of these people from Croatia?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-O37 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know exactly about this case because I was not in the government -- oh, yes. Yes. I'm sorry. I was. They were not prepared for any kind to return to that area. They were not. The government was against the return of refugees all the time. I know that because I had proposed that the Serbs return, but they did not have any understanding for that proposal either.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Thank you. That's enough for the documents. Do you know whether the former SAO Slavonia, Baranja, and Western Srem worked on the demilitarisation issue or the return of the refugees? You didn't hear me?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-O37 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't hear this. Now I can.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-O37 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Could I please have translation of what you said once again, because I didn't hear it.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: I will ask it again. Did the authorities in the former SAO Slavonia, Baranja, and Western Srem work towards demilitarisation and the return of refugees in their region?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-O37 [Resumed]
utterances.text: They did not.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: What did they do?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-O37 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, they kept the state of affairs that was there. That is to say, that the Croats could not return to the area, and refugees from Western Slavonia lived there, those who had fled from there and from other parts of Croatia. They were opposed to the return of Croats to that area.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And what about demilitarisation in this region?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-O37 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Again, they were not demilitarised. The situation remained as it was except that there was no more JNA military presence, only the local people were there. But the equipment remained behind.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Did the authorities in Yugoslavia or Serbia, did they support the course taken by Western Slavonia?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-O37 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, we never got clear-cut support.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: What about the support for Knin and Eastern Slavonia?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-O37 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I think that they had more understanding.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: You say "I think." What is it based on, your thinking?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-O37 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, because I think that we in Western Slavonia who were in favour of things that made us advance further, we would have received support for that. And if the Krajina people were in favour of that, they would not have been supported either. And we also see that there was close contact between the Republic of Srpska Krajina and Belgrade, so that does mean that they did support them.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Because of Western Slavonia, you said already that when the new military commander came, there was a change. Were the political organs stopped doing their work towards the Vance Plan aims?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-O37 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, Western Slavonia was then divided. The Okucani wing opted for the hard-line option, that is to say militarisation again, while the municipal authorities in Pakrac continued within the framework of their abilities that were limited to cooperate with international forces on the expansion of zones, et cetera. They pursued a more normal policy - perhaps I can put it that way - in order to have the situation become calmer. And then in Western Slavonia, there was more army and police. And the regional committee got a man to head it who was close to army and police circles and then they did work in favour of that option.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Was there an Assembly meeting in Western Slavonia on the 24th of February, 1993?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-O37 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That was a meeting of the Assembly of Western Slavonia that discussed the Daruvar agreement that had been signed on the 18th of February, 1992. Yes, the 18th of February.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Did anything happen during this Assembly meeting?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-O37 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, during this Assembly meeting, because there were positive views regarding this agreement, at one point in time the building where the Assembly meeting was taking place was encircled. These special units came. They really liked names like this, special police, special units, et cetera. This unit was headed by Miscevic, and they were issuing threats, namely that they would shoot all of us inside if the Assembly were to decide that way. So people slowly started leaving the Assembly building out of fear so that this would not happen. We wanted to avoid this incident and we therefore recommended that the Assembly do not adopt such a document only to avoid this situation. However, people did feel that the Daruvar agreement did present a solution for them.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: When you say a special unit, are these military units or police units, or can you say?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-O37 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it was something between the police and the military. I could never understand what they really were.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: You have already mentioned that militarisation started again. How was that financed? Do you know that? How did the people in Western Slavonia get money for this?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-O37 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, everything went through Knin. Knin, at that time, financed the police, the military, the local authorities.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Did you ever hear about a Z4 plan?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-O37 [Resumed]
utterances.text: A Z4 plan? Yes. Yes, I did hear about that.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: What was that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-O37 [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was a plan of the international representatives for resolving the Krajina area issues within Croatia. Certain autonomous rights were given to this area then, which was called the RSK. It also dealt with the position of the police and a certain form of autonomy in terms of the political aspect and territorial aspect. I have forgotten the details, but this was a proposal put forth by the international community in order to resolve the status of the Krajina area within Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: When was this Z4 plan discussed?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-O37 [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was first mentioned at the beginning of 1995. First of all just a bit and then more so through the media. As far as I know, it was not officially discussed by the Assembly of Krajina because the top people of the Krajina were against this Z4 plan. It was rejected outright, that they would not accept it, that they would not even debate it. They would not even read it, look at it. And this was done by the president of the republic, Milan Martic.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: How do you know that? Did you hear him reject that plan?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-O37 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I saw that on television when he rejected to comment upon it. At that time, I was no longer in Krajina. By then, I was already in Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Did -- did Mr. Milosevic have a position to the Z4 plan? Do you know that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-O37 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, what I had heard from others -- let me say first of all that I personally considered that Milan Martic didn't wish to accept the agreement and that perhaps he received from friends proposals of this kind. But later on, I heard from one of the Foreign Ministers at the Krajina, Milivoje-Misa Vojnovic that what -- that President Milosevic proposed that the plan not be adopted. And those were his words. And I also heard from others and -- the fact that they didn't want Martic to accept this. But I understood it that Martic didn't want to do so for his own reasons, but I've just told you what I heard.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: When did Mr. Vojinovic mention Mr. Milosevic in this context?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-O37 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I heard that somewhere towards the end of 1997, Milivoje-Misa Vojnovic say that because I asked him personally why this wasn't accepted straight away, because he was the Foreign Minister and only later on through his activities did he become engaged in this, when it was drawing to a close.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Witness, you have mentioned now Milan Martic quite a lot. What was his position before the war?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-O37 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Before the war, he worked in the police force in Knin. I don't know whether he was police chief or a commander or whatever, but I know that he worked in the police in Knin.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: What was his reputation?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-O37 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, he became famous on the 17th of August, 1990. That's when he made a name for himself when he cut off the access roads to Knin. Otherwise, he was prone to anger. He was very explosive by nature and often quarreled. He was quarrelsome. And I think that the tasks that he undertook, and assignments, if I can say so, he wasn't qualified to carry them out. He had very limited education and training for those types of activities, if I may say so.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: What was his attitude towards Croats?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-O37 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, he ranged from being indifferent to adverse. He didn't want to have any talks with them, negotiations with them. He said they could not be trusted and things like that. That was at the other end of the scale.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: The Martic police, when -- do you know when it was founded?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-O37 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I think it was sometime in the summer of 1990.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And in -- how did it develop through the years?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-O37 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it developed from Knin slowly towards Dalmatia and Lika and then to Banija and Kordun as things came to a head, and then encompassed the area of Knin itself and part of Lika, and later on in the war, it spread to Banija and Kordun.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: In the years when the RSK existed, was the Martic police -- were they active throughout the entire territory?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-O37 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, they were. The RSK did act throughout the territory.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: The original Martic police, who trained them?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-O37 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, at the time, there was a lot written about it in the press, actually, and that it was Captain Dragan in that area, Captain Dragan who helped him and trained him and so on.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: You have this information only from the media or do you have an insight into the relationship of the two?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-O37 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mostly from the media, and later on in Knin, I saw that Martic didn't really like Captain Dragan much, although he was not down there when I was in Knin. But when Captain Dragan's name was mentioned, he would grimace and sort of let it be known that he did not acknowledge him as an expert of any kind.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Were any officials from Belgrade involved with the Martic police? Do you know that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-O37 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know that. I didn't see them, so I can't say.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Did Mr. Martic ever refer to some officials?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-O37 [Resumed]
utterances.text: On one occasion he did mention some. I heard Frenki mentioned. He said he was angry with him and his relationship towards the police and to people, but I don't remember anybody else.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Who was angry, Martic or Frenki?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-O37 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Martic was angry.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And when did you hear this remark from Martic?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-O37 [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was sometime in 1992.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: The -- did Mr. -- did the Martic police and did Mr. Martic also control the police in Eastern Slavonia?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-O37 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I think that in Eastern Slavonia, a part of the men were not under their control. There were incidents with Arkan's men, members of his unit or the police, and there were incidents between Martic and Goran Hadzic who allegedly was defending Arkan's men over there.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: When did you get this information and what kind of information?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-O37 [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was at the end of 1992. And this is what it was about. They were people who were outside Milan Martic's control. They weren't accountable to him, but they were accountable to Arkan, and he didn't agree that they should be independent and autonomous and should act in the region without his control.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And was an agreement found? Did -- was that situation ever solved?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-O37 [Resumed]
utterances.text: While I was in the government, there were clashes all the time, and I didn't hear of any agreement.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: You have mentioned for the SAO Krajina the president, Milan Babic. Did he control Martic and his police force?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-O37 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Milan Babic liked to introduce absolutism, that he was the supreme power over one and all. But knowing Milan Martic, I doubt that he was fully under his control because he liked to be fairly free too, whereas Milan Babic did like to issue decrees and proclaim himself to be lord and master over one and all.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Did Milan Martic have control over the TO forces in the SAO Krajina? Do you know that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-O37 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know that.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Milan Martic became -- did he become president of the RSK at some point in time?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-O37 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, he did. I think that was at the beginning of 1994.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Did you see parts of his election campaign?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-O37 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did see them and heard about them. At the time, he would come to Western Slavonia and engage in his presidential campaign there.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: What was Martic's position regarding the future of the RSK and his own future?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-O37 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, he always had the idea of forming an alliance of Serb lands, and on several occasions an assembly of that kind would be held between the Republika Srpska and Republika Srpska Krajina, and in his presidential campaign, whether because he wanted to win the elections or because he wanted to actually do so, he would say that he would hand over his presidential office to President Slobodan Milosevic in a short space of time so that he could be the sole president. That was what the slogan was during his presidential campaign.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Did Mr. Milosevic react to such slogans?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-O37 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't hear that.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Did the Belgrade media support Mr. Martic during this election campaign?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-O37 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, they gave him quite a lot of coverage.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: The Martic police, were they -- do you know whether they were involved in crimes against the Croatian population?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-O37 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I heard down there that in those actions and fighting, there were operations of that kind, but I only heard that from the media. I can't say.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: While you were in the RSK position that you had then, did you ever notice that Martic dismissed or punished any of his police staff for crimes committed against Croats?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-O37 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I didn't hear anything like that.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: With the help of the usher, I would like to show the witness Exhibit C3971, it's tab 20. It has also a B number for Bosnian document. It's both, for both sections.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Witness, it is a letter of the Secretariat of Interior, Vukovar, dated the 3rd of August, 1992, to the MUP in Knin. Do you know -- and it's signed -- it's signed by a person, Dragan Lalic -- Lazic. Sorry; Lazic. Do you know this person Dragan Lazic?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-O37 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Reference is made to a Special Purpose Unit called Red Tigers. Do you know any unit with that name related to the village of Ernestinovo

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-O37 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I just heard about the Red Tigers and Arkan as their leader, but I don't know what place this was linked to, what Erdut or Ernestinovo. I can't say that now. I think it was connected to Erdut most probably. I don't know why, but that seems to be my recollection.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: What was in Erdut?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-O37 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Erdut was also a base where Arkan was stationed.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: You say "also a base." Was Arkan stationed in other places as well?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-O37 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think he had some others as well. At least, according to what I heard, but I don't know where. Quite possibly it was in this place Ernestinovo as well.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Did you ever go to the training or base in Erdut?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-O37 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: How, then, do you know about the base in Erdut?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-O37 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, when we had a government meeting in Erdut, I heard about it. I heard that Arkan was there, was located there.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Ms. Uertz-Retzlaff, I'm sure you have it in mind, but you have quarter of an hour left.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Witness, you have already mentioned the JNA in Western Slavonia. Do you know how the JNA cooperated or if they cooperated with Martic police?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-O37 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know about that.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: You mentioned the arrival of the JNA in Western Slavonia. Who was Jovan Trbojevic?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-O37 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Jovan Trbojevic was an officer of the Yugoslav People's Army who had come sometime after the 31st of October, I think, to the region of Zvecevo. He was a native of a village near Virovitica, and he arrived with some of his volunteers from Novi Sad. Then after a few days, he took over command in Western Slavonia, and it was not functioning at the time. It had been disbanded because the former commander and several members had in fact left Western Slavonia and their commands there.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Who -- do you know who sent Mr Trbojevic to Western Slavonia?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-O37 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, on one occasion he said that he had come there following orders from Kadijevic, General Kadijevic.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: When did he say that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-O37 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that was at the beginning, when he arrived. That's how he introduced himself and that's what he said in order to establish his authority.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: With the help of the usher, I would like to show the witness the Exhibit C4236.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Tab 23.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Sorry. Sorry. I misspoke. 4328. I'm sorry; 4328.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Tab 24.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Your Honour, unfortunately, the translation -- the translation that you have in your binder shows illegible throughout, but looking at the B/C/S version it's actually quite readable. So -- I was just informed you've got another one. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Witness, this document is dated the 16th of October, 1991. Who is the -- it's the TO staff of Western Slavonia and it is a report of the Ministry of Defence. Looking at the document, if you look through the documents, can you tell us what it is?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-O37 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't see very well, but as far as I can see, it is a report on the situation, although I'm not quite clear what this document is about. It lists the distribution of units, deployment of units, according to the staff, the battalions, the fighters, and so on, in Western Slavonia.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And looking at the municipalities that are listed in these documents and their commanders, are they correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-O37 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, they are.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: That's all in relation to this document.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: You have mentioned actually at the beginning of the -- your testimony that the Serbs fled the region. Can you tell us when the Serbs fled the region?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-O37 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Let me repeat: This took place in several -- at several intervals. The 15th of October, Grubisino Polje to begin with, and one month later, the Daruvar Polje --

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Let me stop you. I think you misunderstood me. Were there several waves of people leaving Croatia through the years? I do not want to go into specifics of Western Slavonia in 1991 but --

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-O37 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: -- were they -- in addition to the 1991 wave, were there other waves leaving the territory?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-O37 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, there were. There were some later on as well.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Yes. And can you tell us about it, but briefly?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-O37 [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was a great gave in 1995 after the Flash and Storm operations.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And the Serbs from Croatia, where did they end up? Where did they go?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-O37 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, a part of them ended up in Republika Srpska, the others in Eastern Slavonia, and another portion again was in Vojvodina or, rather, in Serbia, down there in the south.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: When you say "down there in the south," does that mean Kosovo, or where in the south?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-O37 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right. I mean Kosovo and the area around Kosovo.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: How did the Serbs end up there? Did they go there voluntarily?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-O37 [Resumed]
utterances.text: They didn't leave Krajina voluntarily. And when they did leave, what I heard from them, because I wasn't in the actual column, I was told that they were directed in the direction they were to go. So one portion was sent towards Kosovo, another towards Vojvodina, a third towards Eastern Slavonia. They weren't allowed to go where they wanted to go.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Those who -- who were -- those who went to Vojvodina, did this have an effect on the Croatian population living in Vojvodina?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-O37 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, in these waves of refugees, when they left for Serbia, what happened was a part of the Croats from Vojvodina went to Croatia. So they exchanged houses with the Serbs. They exchanged their properties. They would come to Croatia and the Serbs would go to Serbia. Or they sold their houses, their properties.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Did the Croatians leave the Vojvodina voluntarily or were they expelled?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-O37 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, there were cases where there were excessive incidents and where they were actually expelled. I heard about these. But some of them, because of the general climate that prevailed during the war, although no pressure, specific pressure was exerted on them, they decided to leave too. And I also heard that the police would prevent incidents from taking place in Vojvodina, the Serb police, they prevented these incidents, but that people, out of fear, because they were frightened, did leave. I heard that too.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Did you -- did Croats from Vojvodina arrive in Western Slavonia??

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-O37 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Some of them came to Western Slavonia too, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Where did you meet these people, or did you have contacts with them?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-O37 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I talked to some of them when they came to exchange their property. But at the time, they weren't ready to negotiate or have talks. They were very nervous, they were unhappy, and they wanted to find a place a live. That was their prime concern.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Refugees who fled -- Serb refugees who fled Western Slavonia and went to Serbia, were they arrested at some point in time? Do you know that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-O37 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Those who went towards Eastern Slavonia, those were arrested by Arkan's police or, how shall I call them, Arkan's men, they were beaten. I heard a lot about that. Not one story but many stories bandied about, how about how they were belittled and beaten.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Did you speak with victims of such actions?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-O37 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Some of my compatriots from Pakrac. I talked to some of them.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: When were they arrested and beaten by Arkan's? Do you know that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-O37 [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was in 1995, after May. Sometime in June. End of May, in June.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Were any of them arrested in Serbia, by the police in Serbia?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-O37 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I heard that some of them had been arrested and sent to the front in Knin. I heard that too. I don't know which police did this.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Witness, you have told us how you tried over many years to struggle for the Serb issues with peaceful means, and you have also told us about consequences that you suffered in this process. Did you ever give up?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-O37 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, never.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Can you explain that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-O37 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, all my activities so far are geared in that direction. Everything I have done up until now I do now. I wanted to have everything solved by peaceful means. I wanted to avoid conflicts as far as was possible. I wanted people to live normally. I'm now engaged in a programme to bring refugees back and to normalise relations between the Serbs and the Croats, because I know that we have to live together in the region, that that is the imperative concern, and that all prejudice should be done away with and conditions be created for the flow of refugees. Many people wish to go back although there are many problems which prevent them from doing so. So those are the areas I'm working in now.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And in this work, did you ever get any support from the Belgrade authorities?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C-O37 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not any significant support. It is just in this last year or two that I can say that we have been receiving support from the authorities in Belgrade, and we're working towards the return of refugees and to bringing life back to normal again.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Your Honour, these are all my questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Thank you. Well, it's time for us to adjourn. Before we do adjourn, one thing about maps; I think, having heard this evidence, it would be helpful not only to have a map of the relevant part of Croatia but also to have the municipalities marked, because there is evidence about municipalities and we should know where they are. If you could see to that, please. The other point is this: That this courtroom is apparently available on Thursday afternoon, and we are minded to sit Thursday afternoon as well as Thursday morning, but we will let you know the hours in due course. That's just to give a general warning. We will adjourn now. Witness C-037, I should have said to you, the arrangement appears to be that there is another witness to be heard tomorrow, and it may be the day after too, so would you be back, please, when you're asked, and it may be on Thursday but it may be before then, to complete your evidence. Of course remember what I said about not speaking to anybody about it until it's over. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Tuesday, the 1st day of October, 2002, at 9.00 a.m. 25
